case_info.scenario: A 25-year-old man taking no regular medications presented to clinic with a 1-month history of skin lesions, which began as small painless papules on his face and progressed to vesicles and pustules over 1 week. Two weeks prior to presentation, he received empirical treatment for herpes simplex virus with a 7-day course of acyclovir (400 mg 3 times daily). However, the lesions enlarged, became verrucous, and new ulcerated, papular lesions appeared on his trunk and extremities; he developed fevers to 39 °C (102.2 °F) and malaise. He had no known history of sexually transmitted infections but reported unprotected sex with multiple male partners. He reported recent exposure to a work colleague with active tuberculosis. At presentation, temperature was 37.4 °C (99.3 °F); respirations, 18/min; heart rate, 80/min; and blood pressure, 102/64 mm Hg; oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous facial lesions, ulcerative lesions on his back and limbs, and papular lesions across his body (Figure). He had no mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results revealed normal hemoglobin level, white blood cell count, glucose level, and liver function. A fourth-generation immunoassay test for HIV was positive, CD4 count was 125 cells/mm3, and HIV viral load was 157 000 copies/mL. A fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) result was positive. Results of tests for rapid plasma reagin (RPR), human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and tuberculin purified protein derivative were negative. Bacterial culture of the skin lesions grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus aureus. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the skin lesions were negative, and chest radiography findings were normal.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

The patient has disseminated skin lesions with verrucous and ulcerative features, fevers, and a positive FTA-ABS, which strongly suggests disseminated syphilis, possibly malignant syphilis, as the primary driver of his current illness. case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."

       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

   Definition:

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

A 25-year-old man taking no regular medications presented to clinic with a 1-month history of skin lesions, which began as small painless papules on his face and progressed to vesicles and pustules over 1 week. Two weeks prior to presentation, he received empirical treatment for herpes simplex virus with a 7-day course of acyclovir (400 mg 3 times daily). However, the lesions enlarged, became verrucous, and new ulcerated, papular lesions appeared on his trunk and extremities; he developed fevers to 39 °C (102.2 °F) and malaise. He had no known history of sexually transmitted infections but reported unprotected sex with multiple male partners. He reported recent exposure to a work colleague with active tuberculosis. At presentation, temperature was 37.4 °C (99.3 °F); respirations, 18/min; heart rate, 80/min; and blood pressure, 102/64 mm Hg; oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous facial lesions, ulcerative lesions on his back and limbs, and papular lesions across his body (Figure). He had no mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results revealed normal hemoglobin level, white blood cell count, glucose level, and liver function. A fourth-generation immunoassay test for HIV was positive, CD4 count was 125 cells/mm3, and HIV viral load was 157 000 copies/mL. A fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) result was positive. Results of tests for rapid plasma reagin (RPR), human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and tuberculin purified protein derivative were negative. Bacterial culture of the skin lesions grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus aureus. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the skin lesions were negative, and chest radiography findings were normal.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Left, Crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous lesions on patient’s face. Right, Ulcerative lesions on back.
case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

   Definition:

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

1. Mental Demand

       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"

       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.

       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

       pleuritic pain."

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.
